Family Health

Dermabrasion: benefits, preparation and recovery

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Dermabrasion can soften selected scars and surface changes, but it creates a wound that needs careful recovery. Understanding the exact procedure and your individual skin risks is more useful than choosing a treatment by name alone.

What dermabrasion changes

Dermabrasion is a medical resurfacing procedure in which a clinician uses a powered abrasive instrument to remove controlled layers of skin. It is often performed on the face. As the surface heals, some scars or uneven areas may become less noticeable. The aim is improvement in texture or appearance, not the complete removal of every mark or the prevention of future ageing.

Microdermabrasion is a different, much more superficial treatment. Its effects, discomfort and recovery are not interchangeable with surgical dermabrasion. A pharmacy scrub or home exfoliating device is not a slower version of the same operation. Trying to imitate deep resurfacing at home can cause injury, infection and lasting changes in skin colour.

Reasons a specialist might consider it

Potential uses include selected acne scars, scars after injury or surgery, fine wrinkles and areas of sun-damaged or unevenly pigmented skin. The depth and type of the mark matter: a depressed scar, a raised scar and a brown age spot are different problems. Ask which feature is likely to improve and which will remain. A changing or unusual spot needs a diagnosis before cosmetic treatment.

Specialists may also use resurfacing in selected cases of rhinophyma, which causes thickened tissue on the nose, or for certain precancerous skin changes. These are medical indications, not reasons to sand a lesion yourself. Dermabrasion has historically been used for tattoos, but laser techniques and other alternatives often offer a more appropriate approach. Peels, lasers, scar procedures or no procedure may better fit the particular concern.

Skin tone, scars and conditions that affect suitability

The consultation should include an examination, medical history and discussion of realistic results. Active inflammatory acne, an infection or recurrent cold sores may require treatment or a different plan. Previous radiation injury, burns and substantial scarring can affect healing. Tell the clinician about unusually raised scars or keloids, slow wound healing and any treatment that has made your skin fragile.

Darker skin is not automatically unsuitable, but a change in pigmentation may be more noticeable or persistent. Ask about the clinician’s experience treating your skin tone and whether another option carries less risk. The location and depth of treatment also matter. Photographs and a clear explanation of likely improvement can help you decide whether the expected benefit is worth the recovery and possibility of a new mark.

Review medicines and plan preparation individually

Bring a list of prescriptions, nonprescription pain medicines, vitamins and herbal products. Some affect bleeding, skin sensitivity or healing. Do not stop an essential medicine on your own: the prescriber and treating clinician should agree on any change. Report current or recent isotretinoin, even if the course has ended. Evidence about superficial procedures does not establish that powered mechanical dermabrasion is safe during isotretinoin treatment.

A past-year isotretinoin history may prompt a delay or an alternative, but a universal waiting rule for every cosmetic procedure is misleading. Ask for a decision specific to this treatment. Also mention pregnancy or plans to conceive before starting any preparatory medicine. An antiviral may be prescribed to reduce cold-sore recurrence; antibiotics or a retinoid cream are sometimes used for particular reasons. None should be started as a routine home preparation without instructions.

Prepare your skin and arrange practical support

Smoking can interfere with blood flow and wound healing. Discuss stopping sufficiently before the procedure and staying smoke-free through recovery; the service may advise a period of weeks. If stopping is difficult, ask for support early. Avoid tanning and sunburn, and tell the clinic about recent sun exposure. Some preparation plans call for careful sun avoidance for roughly two months beforehand, but the required interval depends on your skin and procedure.

Ask about cleansing, skincare products and when to stop irritating treatments. Arrange transport if you will receive sedation or another anaesthetic that affects alertness. Planning childcare, meals and time away from work is useful when your face will be sore or covered by dressings. Before treatment, obtain written aftercare, a contact number and a clear explanation of the appointments needed to monitor healing.

What happens during treatment

Dermabrasion can be performed in a properly equipped clinic or surgical setting. Local anaesthetic numbs the area; sedation or general anaesthesia may be used for more extensive treatment. Discuss the expected sensations, pain control and risks of the proposed anaesthetic beforehand. You should not have to endure uncontrolled pain simply because the procedure is described as outpatient treatment.

The clinician, sometimes with an assistant, holds the skin steady while moving a powered abrasive wheel or brush over the planned area. The attachment and approach may change around contours such as the mouth. Depth is controlled by clinical judgment, and larger areas may be treated in stages. A protective dressing is applied afterward. A next-day review is part of some plans, but confirm your actual follow-up rather than assuming a standard schedule.

Expect a healing wound before the final result

Early swelling, pinkness or redness, tenderness, tingling and a burning sensation can occur. The treated surface may release a little clear or yellowish fluid and form crusts. That does not make every yellow discharge harmless: increasing pain, spreading warmth, pus, fever or a bad smell needs prompt contact with the clinic. Ask which appearance is expected for the depth of your treatment.

New skin remains delicate after the surface closes. Many people allow around two weeks before returning to work, but the nature of the job, visibility of the area and extent of treatment change that estimate. Pinkness may last several months and fade gradually; three months is not a guaranteed finish date. Assessing the final result too early can be misleading because swelling and colour are still changing.

Clean gently and protect the new surface

Follow the prescribed dressing and cleansing routine. This may involve a moist protective dressing and a specified ointment, such as plain petroleum jelly, rather than letting the wound crack and dry out. Wash your hands before care and avoid picking, scrubbing or pulling off crusts. Ask when makeup, shaving, usual moisturisers and active skincare ingredients can safely return.

Protect the healing area from sunlight with the measures your clinician recommends; sunscreen belongs on skin that is ready for it, not as a substitute for wound care. Ongoing sun protection may be needed for six to twelve months. Swimming, vigorous activity and contact sports can require longer restrictions than desk work. Get specific clearance, particularly if an activity rubs the skin or exposes it to contaminated water.

Understand temporary changes and lasting complications

Possible problems include acne-like bumps or milia, temporary enlargement in the appearance of pores, persistent redness, a rash or swelling. Freckles may fade or disappear in the treated area, and the skin can become darker or lighter than surrounding skin. Bleeding, infection and reactions to medicines or anaesthesia are additional risks. Individual likelihood depends on the treatment and your health.

Scarring is uncommon but can be lasting. New raised, increasingly itchy or thickened areas should be reviewed rather than repeatedly exfoliated. A clinician may recommend treatment such as a steroid for an abnormal scar, but applying a steroid to a fresh wound without advice is not appropriate. Keep scheduled reviews even when healing seems satisfactory, and contact the service sooner for a concerning change.

Decide with clear expectations

Before agreeing, ask what experience the practitioner has, what improvement they expect for your particular scar or skin change, and what alternatives exist. Discuss cost, likely number of sessions, recovery support and the plan if pigmentation or scarring occurs. A procedure that improves one feature can still introduce another problem, so photographs should be considered alongside risks and limitations.

You can take time to decide or choose not to proceed. If treatment goes ahead, the most useful preparation is a personalised plan you can actually follow, including medicine instructions, sun protection, wound care and a way to reach the team. A smoother surface is a possible outcome; a completely mark-free face or permanent freedom from ageing is not a realistic promise.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Surgical dermabrasion, microdermabrasion and home exfoliation have different depths and risks.

Procedure choice, medicine timing and wound care require individual clinical advice.

How BeMama can help

Write down the result you hope for, the help you will need during recovery and the questions you want answered before deciding.

When to seek help

Contact the treating service promptly for worsening pain, spreading redness, pus, fever or an abnormal raised scar. Breathing difficulty or collapse after a medicine requires emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A diagnosis comes before resurfacing an unusual spot.
  • Pigment and scar risks vary with skin and procedure.
  • Report recent isotretinoin and all medicines.
  • Healing and sun protection continue after returning to work.

Frequently asked questions

Is dermabrasion the same as microdermabrasion?

No. Dermabrasion removes deeper layers as a medical procedure. Microdermabrasion acts much more superficially and has different effects and downtime.

Can I reproduce it with a home device?

No. Home exfoliation is not surgical dermabrasion. Trying to remove deeper skin yourself can lead to infection, scarring and pigment changes.

Will it remove every acne scar?

No. Improvement depends on the scar’s type, depth and location. Ask which marks may respond and whether another treatment is better suited.

Does having darker skin rule it out?

Not automatically. Pigment changes need careful discussion with a clinician experienced in your skin tone, and another procedure may be preferable.

Why mention isotretinoin if I finished it already?

It may affect the treatment plan. Research about superficial or manual techniques does not give blanket clearance for powered mechanical dermabrasion.

Should I stop blood-thinning medicines myself?

No. Ask the treating clinician and prescriber to agree on any change so that bleeding risk is balanced against the reason for the medicine.

Will I need general anaesthesia?

Not always. Local anaesthetic is common, while sedation or general anaesthesia may suit more extensive treatment. Confirm the plan and transport requirements.

Is yellow fluid always an infection?

A small amount of wound fluid can occur during healing. Pus, a bad smell, fever or increasing pain needs prompt review rather than diagnosis from colour alone.

Can I go straight back to my usual skincare?

No. Follow instructions for dressings, gentle cleansing and when to restart products, shaving and makeup. Avoid picking or scrubbing the healing surface.

When will my skin look settled?

The surface may heal before redness and pigment settle. Return to work is often possible around two weeks, while colour changes can take months; your clinician should give an individual estimate.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
